name: Leadership Communication
description: Develop the communication skills of effective leaders — public speaking, active listening, team communication, conflict resolution, negotiation, cross-cultural communication, and leading with influence.

modules.title: What Is Leadership?
modules.objectives: Compare trait, situational, transformational, and servant-leadership models; identify what each model emphasizes and leaves unexplained; use evidence from a scenario to justify a context-sensitive leadership choice.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 12.2 — treats leadership as an interaction among leaders, followers, context, process, and outcomes rather than as a single settled formula.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — Simon Sinek: How Great Leaders Inspire Action
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 1: What Is Leadership? Reviews leadership as a context-dependent process and compares major models without treating any one model as a universal law.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management, 13.6 — compare situational and contingency approaches, including their assumptions and limitations.
modules.assignment: Solo case analysis (650–800 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use this supplied scenario: A four-person student media team must publish a safety-information video in five days. Mina is technically skilled but new to the topic; Rafael understands the topic but misses deadlines; Jo is reliable and wants autonomy; Sam has stopped speaking after two ideas were dismissed. Steps: (1) state the team's goal and constraints; (2) analyze the case through any two course models chosen from trait, situational, transformational, and servant leadership; (3) cite three exact details from the scenario; (4) propose four leader actions, with who, when, and intended result; (5) add a 100–150 word limitation note explaining what the models cannot establish. No personal disclosure or outside interview is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: accurate model use 30%, scenario evidence 25%, feasibility and specificity of actions 25%, limitations and clarity 20%.

modules.title: Self-Awareness & Emotional Intelligence
modules.objectives: Define and compare ability-based and competency-based accounts of emotional intelligence; identify observable signs of self-awareness, emotion regulation, and empathy in a supplied scenario; explain and justify a proportionate response while avoiding diagnosis from limited evidence.
modules.readingNote: APA Dictionary of Psychology — concise definition of emotional intelligence and Mayer and Salovey's four-ability model; compare it with the competency labels used in this course.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — Daniel Goleman: Why Aren't We More Compassionate?
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 2: Self-Awareness & Emotional Intelligence. Distinguishes noticing emotion from choosing a response and applies empathy without claiming that an EQ label diagnoses a person.
modules.practiceNote: APA Dictionary of Psychology — use the feelings-wheel concept to move from a broad emotion label to a more precise, non-diagnostic description.
modules.assignment: Solo response plan (500–650 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use this supplied scenario: After receiving a neutral revision request, Noor reads it as a personal attack, drafts an angry reply, and notices a racing heart and narrowed attention. The sender wrote, 'The evidence in sections 2 and 3 does not yet support the conclusion. Please revise by Friday.' Steps: (1) separate observable facts from Noor's interpretations; (2) name two plausible emotions without diagnosing Noor; (3) write a 60–90 word regulated reply; (4) explain two pause-and-check strategies and one empathy question; (5) compare how an ability model and a competency model would describe the response. No self-rating or personal disclosure is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: fact/inference distinction 25%, application of emotion concepts 30%, quality of reply and strategies 30%, model comparison and clarity 15%.

modules.title: Public Speaking Foundations
modules.objectives: Build an audience-centered speech with a purposeful introduction, organized body, and conclusion; apply pacing, pausing, vocal variety, and visible delivery choices; use preparation strategies to manage speaking anxiety.
modules.readingNote: Open Textbook Library — It's About Them: Public Speaking in the 21st Century. Use Chapters 2, 8, 9, and 10 for confidence, organization, delivery, introductions, and conclusions.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — Chris Anderson: TED's Secret to Great Public Speaking
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 3: Public Speaking Foundations. Demonstrates audience-centered structure, delivery choices, and realistic preparation strategies for speaking anxiety.
modules.practiceNote: Open Textbook Library — use Chapters 8–10 as a checklist for outline structure, realistic rehearsal, delivery, introductions, and conclusions.
modules.assignment: Solo briefing package (2–3 minute recording plus a 350–500 word outline and self-review; submit MP4/MOV and PDF/DOCX). Input: use one supplied fictional brief: (A) recycling — new blue bins accept clean paper, metal cans, and plastic bottles starting Monday; contaminated loads are rejected; (B) study zone — Room 204 is reserved for silent study from 3:00–5:00 on Tuesdays and Thursdays; eight seats are available; (C) digital safety — students should use a unique passphrase and verify unexpected login prompts through the official site. Steps: (1) identify the audience and one desired action; (2) write a hook, thesis, two points supported only by the selected brief, transitions, and conclusion; (3) record in one take or as audio over slides; (4) cite timestamps for one effective pause, one delivery strength, and two revisions; (5) include a 75–100 word anxiety-management plan. No live audience or outside research is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: accurate use of supplied facts and audience-purpose alignment 25%, organization 25%, audible/visible delivery 25%, timestamped self-evidence and revision plan 25%.

modules.title: Storytelling for Leaders
modules.objectives: Identify how situation, conflict, change, and resolution shape a narrative; construct an evidence-respecting story for a defined audience; combine human context with data without inventing facts or implying that a story proves causation.
modules.readingNote: Open Textbook Library — Prose Fiction: An Introduction to the Semiotics of Narrative. Use the plot and narration chapters to analyze sequence, conflict, perspective, and resolution.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — Andrew Stanton: The Clues to a Great Story
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 4: Storytelling for Leaders. Connects narrative structure to leadership messages while preserving the boundary between an illustrative story and evidence for a claim.
modules.practiceNote: Our World in Data — Literacy. Use one labeled chart and its source notes to practice explaining a real trend without changing the statistic or claiming unsupported causes.
modules.assignment: Solo evidence-to-story brief (600–750 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use only this supplied dataset: In a fictional district, on-time library returns rose from 62% (Year 1) to 68% (Year 2) and 79% (Year 3) after reminder texts were introduced between Years 2 and 3; no comparison district or causal study is available. Steps: (1) write a 250–350 word fictionalized narrative with situation, tension, turning point, and resolution; (2) include all three values accurately; (3) label invented names/details as illustrative; (4) write a 150–200 word evidence note stating what the data show and do not show; (5) revise one sentence that initially overclaimed causation. No personal story is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: narrative structure 25%, numerical accuracy 25%, evidence/causation boundaries 30%, revision quality and clarity 20%.

modules.title: Active Listening & Empathetic Communication
modules.objectives: Identify listening barriers; distinguish paraphrasing, clarifying, and validating responses; use verbal and nonverbal cues cautiously; demonstrate empathy without assuming unspoken feelings or agreeing with every claim.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 11.5 — explains listening as a core managerial communication channel and connects message meaning to source, purpose, and context.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — William Ury: The Walk from 'No' to 'Yes' (listening & empathy)
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 5: Active Listening & Empathetic Communication. Models paraphrasing, clarification, and validation while warning against mind-reading from a single cue.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 11.1 — trace a message through encoding, medium, decoding, feedback, and noise, then identify where clarification can prevent distortion.
modules.assignment: Solo listening transcript analysis (550–700 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use this supplied statement: 'I submitted the draft Tuesday, but the requirements changed Thursday. Now the group says I am behind. I am frustrated, and I need to know which version is actually due.' Steps: (1) list the speaker's explicit facts, feelings, and request in separate columns; (2) identify two assumptions a listener should not make; (3) write one paraphrase, two open questions, one validation statement that does not claim agreement, and one concise summary; (4) explain how each response reduces a specific listening barrier; (5) revise one response that sounds judgmental. No partner or real disclosure is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: accurate separation of message elements 25%, quality of listening responses 35%, barrier analysis 25%, revision and clarity 15%.

modules.title: Team Communication & Collaboration
modules.objectives: Analyze how roles, norms, status, and information flow affect team communication; explain psychological safety as a shared perception rather than a guarantee of comfort or performance; design observable norms that support participation and accountability.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 10.3 — examines team composition, norms, coaching, accountability, and incremental improvement.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — Amy Edmondson: How to Turn a Group of Strangers into a Team
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 6: Team Communication & Collaboration. Examines roles, norms, participation, trust, and psychological safety as context-dependent team conditions.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 10.4 — use the conflict-response discussion to distinguish constructive disagreement from personal attack or suppressed conflict.
modules.assignment: Solo team-protocol design (700–900 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use this supplied scenario: A remote four-person team has one week to verify 120 records. One member dominates calls, one sends corrections privately after meetings, one misses updates because decisions are scattered across chat, and one notices an error but is unsure whether questions are welcome. Steps: (1) map role, channel, status, and norm problems; (2) identify four exact scenario clues; (3) write five observable communication norms, each with owner, channel, timing, and exception; (4) design a 20-minute meeting agenda and a decision log template; (5) explain why the plan may support, but cannot guarantee, psychological safety or performance. No real team experience is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: diagnosis 25%, protocol specificity 35%, evidence use 20%, calibrated explanation and clarity 20%.

modules.title: Giving & Receiving Feedback
modules.objectives: Use the SBI model as one structured feedback tool; distinguish observation, interpretation, and impact; write behavior-specific, actionable feedback; evaluate feedback for accuracy, fairness, and usefulness before acting on it.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 8.3 — explains how source credibility, perceived accuracy, fairness, and expectations affect whether feedback is accepted and used.
modules.videoNote: TED Talk — LeeAnn Renninger: The Secret to Giving Great Feedback
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 7: Giving & Receiving Feedback. Demonstrates SBI as a useful structure, not a guarantee of a particular reaction, and separates observed behavior from inferred intent.
modules.practiceNote: Center for Creative Leadership — SBI and the SBII extension. Compare observable situation-behavior-impact language with questions about intent rather than assuming intent.
modules.assignment: Solo feedback packet (650–800 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use these supplied cases: (A) During Monday's review, Casey interrupted three times before others finished; two agenda items were not discussed. (B) Priya submitted the checklist one day early with all required fields; the reviewer finished ahead of schedule. (C) A reviewer writes only, 'This is careless.' Steps: (1) write an SBI message for A and B; (2) for each, label situation, observable behavior, and impact; (3) rewrite C into two clarifying questions plus one actionable request; (4) identify one alternative explanation for A so you do not infer intent; (5) write a 100–150 word plan for evaluating feedback before accepting or rejecting it. No subordinate, supervisor, or personal disclosure is required. Submit: the complete deliverable in the file format and length stated at the start of this assignment. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: observation/inference accuracy 30%, SBI construction 30%, actionability and fairness 25%, response plan and clarity 15%.

modules.title: Conflict Resolution & Difficult Conversations
modules.objectives: Use the Thomas-Kilmann framework descriptively rather than as a universal ranking of styles; distinguish positions, interests, options, and alternatives; write de-escalating language; plan a difficult conversation with safety and power differences in mind.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Organizational Behavior, 14.3 — surveys conflict-prevention and conflict-reduction strategies and shows that context affects which response is appropriate.
modules.videoNote: TEDx Talk — The Keys to Productive Conflict. Examine its proposed practices as context-dependent tools and compare them with the module's conflict and negotiation frameworks.
modules.video2Note: GIIS lesson — Leadership Communication, Module 8: Conflict Resolution & Difficult Conversations. Applies conflict-style and interest-based tools while noting that safety, authority, time, and stakes can change the appropriate response.
modules.practiceNote: Harvard Law School Program on Negotiation — distinguish positions, interests, options, objective standards, commitments, and BATNA when preparing a negotiation.
modules.assignment: Solo difficult-conversation plan (800–1,000 words, PDF or DOCX). Input: use this supplied scenario: Two student editors share one lab from 3:00–5:00. Alex needs 50 uninterrupted minutes on a computer with upload access and must finish by 4:00. Blake needs 25 minutes with the editing software, then 10 minutes at the equipment desk before it closes at 4:15. The first computer supports both tasks from 3:00; a second computer with the same software and upload access becomes available at 3:30. A lab manager can confirm a schedule but cannot extend either deadline. Steps: (1) separate each stated position from interests and clearly label any inference; (2) identify each side's realistic alternative if they do not agree; (3) generate three feasible options and compare them using timing and fairness criteria; (4) write a 12–16 line de-escalating conversation script; (5) use the Thomas-Kilmann model to describe two possible approaches and explain when each might fit; (6) add a safety note describing when to pause and seek an adult or institutional process. No real conflict or disclosure is required. Submit: the complete plan in the stated file format and length. Include: every requested scenario-based artifact, exact scenario evidence, analysis step, and limitation or safety note. Evaluation: position/interest/alternative analysis 30%, option quality and criteria 25%, script 25%, context-sensitive framework use and safety 20%.

questions.question: Which leadership theory argues that effective leaders adjust their style based on the readiness and skill level of their followers?
options: Trait Theory
Transformational Leadership
Situational Leadership
Servant Leadership
questions.answer: Situational Leadership
questions.explanation: In the Hersey-Blanchard situational model, leaders vary task and relationship behavior in response to assessed readiness. It is a proposed framework for choosing behavior, not a law that guarantees effectiveness.

questions.question: A leader who prioritizes the needs of their team members above their own authority and focuses on helping others grow is best described as a:
options: Autocratic leader
Servant leader
Laissez-faire leader
Transactional leader
questions.answer: Servant leader
questions.explanation: Greenleaf's servant-leadership model begins with service and emphasizes followers' growth and well-being. The label describes priorities; it does not by itself prove that a leader's decisions are effective or ethical.

questions.question: According to Daniel Goleman, which component of emotional intelligence involves understanding and sharing the feelings of others?
options: Self-regulation
Motivation
Empathy
Social skills
questions.answer: Empathy
questions.explanation: In Goleman's competency model, empathy means attending to and trying to understand other people's feelings and perspectives. Other emotional-intelligence models use different structures, so this item asks specifically about Goleman's terminology.

questions.question: Which preparation step is most likely to help a speaker manage ordinary pre-presentation anxiety?
options: Rehearse aloud under realistic timing and use slow breathing before speaking
Memorize every word and restart whenever one word changes
Avoid looking at the audience or checking the room
Add more content than the time limit permits
questions.answer: Rehearse aloud under realistic timing and use slow breathing before speaking
questions.explanation: Realistic rehearsal reduces uncertainty about structure and timing, while slow breathing can lower physical arousal. These strategies can help with ordinary nervousness but are not a guaranteed or clinical treatment.

questions.question: The narrative arc in storytelling typically includes which sequence of elements?
options: Data, claim, rebuttal, conclusion
Hook, thesis, evidence, call to action
Situation, conflict, turning point, resolution
Introduction, body, summary, question
questions.answer: Situation, conflict, turning point, resolution
questions.explanation: A compelling narrative arc establishes the context (situation), introduces a problem (conflict), shows a change (turning point), and delivers the outcome or lesson (resolution).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes active listening?
options: Waiting silently for your turn to speak
Paraphrasing, asking follow-up questions, and giving full attention to the speaker
Nodding and smiling while thinking about your response
Taking detailed notes without looking at the speaker
questions.answer: Paraphrasing, asking follow-up questions, and giving full attention to the speaker
questions.explanation: Active listening requires complete mental presence, reflective paraphrasing to confirm understanding, and follow-up questions that demonstrate genuine engagement with the speaker's message.

questions.question: Psychological safety on a team is best defined as:
options: Freedom from physical harm in the workplace
A belief that team members can speak up without fear of punishment or humiliation
A policy that prevents all conflict between teammates
Ensuring only positive feedback is shared
questions.answer: A belief that team members can speak up without fear of punishment or humiliation
questions.explanation: Edmondson defines psychological safety as a shared belief that interpersonal risk-taking is safe within a team. Research links it to speaking up and learning in some settings, but it does not eliminate conflict or guarantee performance.

questions.question: In the SBI feedback model, which three elements organize a feedback message?
options: Situation, Behavior, Impact
Subject, Behavior, Impact
Situation, Belief, Intention
Source, Bias, Interpretation
questions.answer: Situation, Behavior, Impact
questions.explanation: SBI prompts the speaker to identify a specific situation, describe observable behavior, and state its impact. It is a communication structure, not proof of the other person's intent or a guarantee of acceptance.

questions.question: Which behavior generally supports attentive listening rather than obstructing it?
options: Prejudging the speaker
Preparing your rebuttal while they speak
Using culturally appropriate attentive cues and asking a clarifying question
Being distracted by your phone
questions.answer: Using culturally appropriate attentive cues and asking a clarifying question
questions.explanation: Attentive cues and clarification support understanding. Appropriate eye contact and body language vary by culture, access need, and setting, so a single nonverbal cue should not be treated as universal proof of listening.

questions.question: Which conflict-handling style involves finding a middle-ground solution where both parties give up something to gain something?
options: Avoiding
Accommodating
Competing
Compromising
questions.answer: Compromising
questions.explanation: Compromising (Thomas-Kilmann model) involves each party partially satisfying their concerns through mutual concessions — a middle-ground approach that is moderately assertive and cooperative.

questions.question: When it is safe and appropriate to give feedback to a more senior person, which approach is most constructive?
options: Avoid giving feedback upward altogether
Frame feedback as a question or observation and focus on shared goals
Send the feedback anonymously to avoid conflict
Wait for a performance review cycle to share your concerns
questions.answer: Frame feedback as a question or observation and focus on shared goals
questions.explanation: A specific observation, a genuine question, and a connection to a shared goal can make upward feedback easier to consider. Power, safety, policy, and available reporting channels still affect whether direct feedback is appropriate.

questions.question: In Goleman's competency model, which component concerns managing disruptive emotions and impulses?
options: Self-regulation
Empathy
Social skill
Motivation
questions.answer: Self-regulation
questions.explanation: Goleman's model uses self-regulation for managing impulses and choosing a response. This is model-specific terminology and should not be treated as a clinical assessment.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the role of body language during a public speech?
options: It supplies cues that audiences may interpret alongside words, voice, and context
It reliably reveals the speaker's private emotional state
It proves whether the speaker's evidence is accurate
It carries one fixed meaning across cultures and access needs
questions.answer: It supplies cues that audiences may interpret alongside words, voice, and context
questions.explanation: Posture, gesture, expression, and movement can shape audience interpretation, but no single cue reliably reveals intelligence, truthfulness, preparation, or emotion. Meanings also vary by person and context.

questions.question: Describe the difference between trait leadership theory and situational leadership theory. Give one specific example of how each theory would explain a leader's success or failure, and name one context factor or limitation for each explanation.
questions.answer: Exemplar: A trait approach would examine whether a coordinator's persistence and dependability help explain why others accept direction. A situational approach would examine whether the coordinator changes task guidance and support when a novice becomes more capable. The first emphasizes relatively stable characteristics; the second emphasizes fit between behavior and circumstances. Neither example proves that the model alone caused success.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for accurately contrasting the models' focal variables; 1 point for two specific, logically matched examples plus a limitation or context note.

questions.question: A teammate gives you blunt, critical feedback on a presentation you worked hard on. Using what you know about receiving feedback and emotional intelligence, describe how you would respond in the moment and how you would process it afterward.
questions.answer: Exemplar: Pause and say, 'I want to understand. Which slide or behavior created the problem, and what outcome did you expect?' If the exchange is safe, summarize the answer before responding. Later, separate the wording from the claim, check the feedback against the presentation criteria or recording, identify one supported revision, and set aside claims that remain vague or inaccurate. Follow up only if clarification would be useful.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for an in-the-moment response that shows regulation and clarification without automatic agreement; 1 point for an afterward process that checks evidence, selects an action, and accounts for safety or credibility.

questions.question: In Simon Sinek's 'Start With Why' model, which message order is proposed as a way to inspire action?
options: Communicating purpose or belief before explaining how and what
Explaining what they do in detail
Withholding the purpose until the audience agrees
Replacing evidence with an emotional slogan
questions.answer: Communicating purpose or belief before explaining how and what
questions.explanation: Sinek's model recommends beginning with purpose, then explaining process and product. It is a persuasive framework presented in the talk, not a demonstrated rule that every effective leader must follow.

questions.question: A leader who consistently keeps promises, admits mistakes, and shares information openly is building which foundation of team trust?
options: Competence-based trust
Integrity-based trust
Benevolence-based trust
Authority-based trust
questions.answer: Integrity-based trust
questions.explanation: Integrity-based trust is built through honesty, consistency, and transparency. It differs from competence trust (skill-based) and benevolence trust (caring about others' welfare).

questions.question: A team member rarely speaks in live meetings but submits careful written objections afterward. What is the best first response?
options: Ask which participation channels help them contribute and offer an advance written agenda
Assume silence means agreement with every decision
Require spontaneous speaking without advance notice
Explain the behavior entirely by the person's nationality
questions.answer: Ask which participation channels help them contribute and offer an advance written agenda
questions.explanation: The response gathers individual evidence and reduces a process barrier without stereotyping. Silence can have many causes, including timing, status, language, access needs, or reflection style.

questions.question: BATNA in negotiation stands for:
options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
Baseline Agreement Terms and Negotiations Approach
Best Approach To Neutral Alternatives
Balanced Agreement Through Negotiated Action
questions.answer: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
questions.explanation: BATNA is the best realistic course available if no agreement is reached. Identifying it supports comparison and preparation; merely naming a BATNA does not automatically create leverage or determine a fair outcome.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a story responsibly alongside evidence?
options: This fictional example illustrates one possible experience; the dataset shows the trend but not its cause
This one person's experience proves the program works for everyone
Because the story is emotional, no source note is needed
The narrative may change the reported values to improve the ending
questions.answer: This fictional example illustrates one possible experience; the dataset shows the trend but not its cause
questions.explanation: A responsible communicator labels illustration versus observation and preserves the limits of the evidence. Narrative can clarify significance, but it cannot turn correlation or a single case into causal proof.

questions.question: A speaker says, 'The instructions changed after I submitted, and I need to know which version counts.' Which response best demonstrates active listening?
options: So you submitted before the change and want clarification about the required version; is that right?
You are overreacting because revisions are normal
I already know what happened, so there is no need to clarify
Let me explain why my own workload is harder
questions.answer: So you submitted before the change and want clarification about the required version; is that right?
questions.explanation: The response paraphrases the stated facts and request, then checks accuracy. It does not diagnose emotion, assign blame, or shift attention to the listener.

questions.question: An effective meeting agenda should include:
options: A list of attendees only
Topics, time allocations, and owners for each agenda item
Only items that require unanimous approval
A detailed recap of the previous month's results
questions.answer: Topics, time allocations, and owners for each agenda item
questions.explanation: Topics, time boxes, and owners clarify preparation and process. They can improve meeting focus, but results also depend on facilitation, participation, decision rules, and follow-through.

questions.question: In principled negotiation (Getting to Yes), which of the following is a core principle?
options: Focus on positions, not interests
Make the other party feel they lost something
Separate people from the problem
Use emotional pressure to gain concessions
questions.answer: Separate people from the problem
questions.explanation: The principled-negotiation framework advises separating relationship issues from the substantive problem. It also emphasizes interests, options, and objective criteria; context and power differences still matter in application.

questions.question: Which feedback statement most clearly separates observed behavior from inferred intent?
options: During today's review, you spoke while Mira was presenting; she restarted the explanation twice
You interrupted because you do not respect Mira
You always try to control every discussion
Your attitude made the meeting bad
questions.answer: During today's review, you spoke while Mira was presenting; she restarted the explanation twice
questions.explanation: The answer anchors the message to a specific situation and observable actions. It avoids claiming to know motive or turning one event into a fixed personality judgment.

questions.question: Why should a leader avoid treating one leadership framework as a universal law?
options: Leadership outcomes also depend on followers, task, context, power, and implementation
Frameworks are useful only when they predict every outcome
A model becomes a law once it has a memorable name
Context matters only for inexperienced leaders
questions.answer: Leadership outcomes also depend on followers, task, context, power, and implementation
questions.explanation: Frameworks select and organize variables; they do not capture every causal factor or guarantee results. A sound application states the model's assumptions and checks the fit with available evidence.

questions.question: Interest-based negotiation differs from positional bargaining because it:
options: Focuses on what each party demands rather than why
Explores the underlying needs behind each party's stated position
Avoids any compromise
Relies on a mediator to decide the outcome
questions.answer: Explores the underlying needs behind each party's stated position
questions.explanation: Interest-based negotiation asks why a stated demand matters and may reveal tradeoffs or compatible needs. It can expand options, but it does not ensure agreement, equal power, or a mutually beneficial result.

questions.question: Which facilitation practice best creates a low-pressure opportunity for quieter participants to contribute?
options: Share the prompt in advance and invite either a written response or a passable round-robin turn
Call on the same person repeatedly until they answer aloud
Treat silence as consent and close the decision immediately
Require the quietest person to lead without notice
questions.answer: Share the prompt in advance and invite either a written response or a passable round-robin turn
questions.explanation: Advance notice, multiple channels, and permission to pass broaden access without forcing disclosure. No technique guarantees participation, so facilitators should check preferences and preserve accountability through clear follow-up.

questions.question: In the Thomas-Kilmann model, which behavior most clearly illustrates the avoiding style?
options: Refusing to discuss the issue and changing the subject
Yielding to preserve the relationship
Pressing for one's preferred outcome
Exploring both parties' concerns together
questions.answer: Refusing to discuss the issue and changing the subject
questions.explanation: The model describes avoiding as low assertiveness and low cooperativeness toward the immediate issue. Avoiding can be harmful when it leaves important problems unresolved, but delay or withdrawal may be appropriate when safety, timing, or low stakes justify it.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the 'hook' at the opening of a leadership presentation?
options: To provide the agenda for the presentation
To introduce all speakers by name
To immediately capture the audience's attention and create curiosity
To summarize the conclusion before the presentation begins
questions.answer: To immediately capture the audience's attention and create curiosity
questions.explanation: A relevant hook directs attention to the topic and gives the audience a reason to keep listening. It should fit the audience and purpose; shock or novelty alone does not make an opening effective.

questions.question: Which response best demonstrates emotional self-regulation after receiving a critical message?
options: Pause, identify the reaction, check the message, and choose a proportionate reply
Suppress every feeling and pretend the message had no effect
Reply immediately so the sender sees the first reaction
Assume the sender intended harm without asking for clarification
questions.answer: Pause, identify the reaction, check the message, and choose a proportionate reply
questions.explanation: Self-regulation involves noticing emotion and managing the response rather than denying emotion. Checking the message and context reduces the risk of acting on an untested interpretation.

questions.question: Which option best describes the aim of the 'Collaborating' style in the Thomas-Kilmann model?
options: One party wins and the other loses
Both parties give up something to meet in the middle
Both parties explore concerns and seek a solution that addresses important interests on both sides
One party gives in to avoid further conflict
questions.answer: Both parties explore concerns and seek a solution that addresses important interests on both sides
questions.explanation: The model places collaborating high on assertiveness and cooperativeness. It aims for joint problem solving, but it takes time and does not guarantee that all concerns can be fully satisfied; another style may fit safety, urgency, or low-stakes conditions better.

questions.question: In a cross-cultural meeting, someone says, 'That may be difficult.' What is the most responsible next step?
options: Ask a neutral clarifying question about the specific concern and possible constraints
Treat the phrase as definite agreement
Treat the phrase as definite refusal based on nationality
Ignore the phrase because indirect language has no meaning
questions.answer: Ask a neutral clarifying question about the specific concern and possible constraints
questions.explanation: The phrase may signal concern, hesitation, or refusal, but context and individual style matter. Clarification tests meaning without converting a cultural tendency into a stereotype about one person.

questions.question: A team reports that approval rose from 60% before a storytelling workshop to 70% afterward, then claims the workshop caused the increase. Which revision is most evidence-bounded?
options: Approval rose after the workshop, but without a comparison group or other causal evidence, the sequence alone does not establish that the workshop caused the change
The workshop caused exactly a 10% improvement for every participant
Because approval increased, no other explanation needs consideration
The percentages should be removed so the story sounds stronger
questions.answer: Approval rose after the workshop, but without a comparison group or other causal evidence, the sequence alone does not establish that the workshop caused the change
questions.explanation: A before-and-after pattern establishes timing, not causation by itself. Other changes may have contributed; a comparison design or additional evidence would be needed to isolate the workshop’s effect.

questions.question: You are a team leader and two members of your team are in an escalating conflict that is affecting team morale. Using the principles of conflict resolution and difficult conversations covered in this course, describe step-by-step how you would intervene. Include which conflict style(s) you would encourage and why.
questions.answer: Exemplar: First assess immediate safety, authority, policy, and whether a neutral adult or formal process is needed. If an informal intervention is appropriate, gather each account without promising secrecy, identify stated positions and underlying interests, verify shared facts, and agree on discussion rules. In a joint meeting, paraphrase each concern, generate options, compare them with objective criteria, document commitments, and schedule follow-up. Collaboration may fit when both can participate safely and time permits; temporary avoidance, accommodation, compromise, or a formal decision may fit different stakes or power conditions.
questions.explanation: Rubric: safety and authority check 20%; clear sequence and listening/de-escalation language 30%; positions, interests, options, and criteria 30%; context-sensitive conflict-style justification and follow-up 20%.

questions.question: Using either your capstone presentation or the supplied alternative below, identify two communication skills demonstrated, cite specific evidence for each, and propose one targeted revision. Supplied alternative: a speaker opens with the claim, presents three accurate data points without source labels, speaks for four minutes without a pause, and ends with a clear request.
questions.answer: Exemplar using the supplied alternative: The ending demonstrates audience-centered purpose because it gives a clear request. The three accurate values provide evidence, but missing source labels weaken credibility. A targeted revision is to add the source and date beside each value and insert a pause after the second point so the audience can process it. A response using the student's capstone should likewise name two course skills, cite observable evidence, and propose a specific revision rather than merely rating the speaker.
questions.explanation: Rubric: two accurately named course skills 30%; specific observable evidence 30%; feasible targeted revision linked to one weakness 30%; clear distinction between observation and self-evaluation 10%.

quizQuestions.question: Which leadership approach primarily examines personal characteristics associated with leader emergence or effectiveness?
options: Situational Leadership
Transformational Leadership
Trait Theory
Servant Leadership
quizQuestions.answer: Trait Theory
quizQuestions.explanation: Trait approaches study characteristics associated with leadership. Early 'great man' accounts emphasized inborn qualities, but modern trait research does not establish that leaders are simply born or that traits operate independently of context and learning.

quizQuestions.question: Servant leadership, as defined by Robert Greenleaf, prioritizes:
options: Accumulating personal power
The growth and well-being of followers
Strict command-and-control management
Short-term organizational profit
quizQuestions.answer: The growth and well-being of followers
quizQuestions.explanation: Greenleaf's servant-leadership model begins with service and emphasizes followers' growth and well-being. This describes the model's priority, not a guaranteed outcome of using the label.

quizQuestions.question: A project leader gives detailed direction to a novice but later shifts to delegation after the novice demonstrates competence. Which model most directly describes this adaptation?
options: Situational Leadership
Transformational Leadership
Trait Theory
Servant Leadership
quizQuestions.answer: Situational Leadership
quizQuestions.explanation: Situational leadership proposes varying task and relationship behavior in response to assessed readiness. The scenario fits that model, although the label alone does not prove the choice will succeed.

quizQuestions.question: Self-awareness in emotional intelligence refers to:
options: Knowing the emotions of others before they express them
Accurately recognizing your own emotions and how they affect your behavior
Controlling your emotions so others cannot see them
Memorizing theories about emotion
quizQuestions.answer: Accurately recognizing your own emotions and how they affect your behavior
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-awareness is the foundation of EQ — without knowing your own emotional patterns, you cannot regulate them or understand their impact on your leadership.

quizQuestions.question: A leader who pauses before responding to an angry email, chooses words carefully, and avoids retaliating is demonstrating:
options: Low empathy
Self-regulation
Social skills
Motivation
quizQuestions.answer: Self-regulation
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-regulation is the ability to manage disruptive emotions and impulses, think before acting, and maintain composure under pressure.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is the best example of empathy in a leadership context?
options: Telling a struggling employee to simply work harder
Understanding a team member's personal challenges and adjusting expectations temporarily
Keeping your own emotions hidden at all times
Delegating emotional issues to HR
quizQuestions.answer: Understanding a team member's personal challenges and adjusting expectations temporarily
quizQuestions.explanation: Empathy means recognizing and understanding the feelings of others and taking their perspective into account when making decisions.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement accurately compares two common approaches to emotional intelligence?
options: Ability models emphasize processing emotional information; competency models group broader learned behaviors
All emotional-intelligence models use the same five components
Ability models diagnose mental-health conditions; competency models do not
Both models claim emotion should always override evidence
quizQuestions.answer: Ability models emphasize processing emotional information; competency models group broader learned behaviors
quizQuestions.explanation: The approaches overlap but organize the construct differently. A course exercise can apply their concepts, but it is not a validated diagnosis or proof of leadership effectiveness.

quizQuestions.question: Which component of a speech is responsible for establishing credibility and previewing the main points?
options: Conclusion
Transition
Introduction
Body
quizQuestions.answer: Introduction
quizQuestions.explanation: An effective introduction grabs attention with a hook, establishes the speaker's credibility, states the thesis, and previews the structure of the speech.

quizQuestions.question: Vocal variety in public speaking refers to changes in:
options: The topic of the speech
Pitch, pace, volume, and tone
Slide design and visuals
The speaker's position on stage
quizQuestions.answer: Pitch, pace, volume, and tone
quizQuestions.explanation: Vocal variety keeps the audience engaged and helps emphasize key points. A monotone voice loses audience attention even when the content is strong.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement about nonverbal communication in a speech is most accurate?
options: Words alone carry 90% of the message
Body language and tone can influence audience perception, but their meaning depends on context
Gestures are a distraction and should be minimized
Eye contact is less important than slide content
quizQuestions.answer: Body language and tone can influence audience perception, but their meaning depends on context
quizQuestions.explanation: Audiences use verbal and nonverbal information together. No fixed percentage applies to every speech, and a cue such as eye contact should not be treated as universal evidence of confidence or honesty.

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary purpose of using storytelling in a leadership communication?
options: To entertain the audience and fill time
To create emotional connection and make ideas memorable
To show off personal experiences
To avoid using data and evidence
quizQuestions.answer: To create emotional connection and make ideas memorable
quizQuestions.explanation: A relevant story can supply context, stakes, and sequence that help an audience follow and remember an idea. It should support rather than replace accurate evidence.

quizQuestions.question: The 'conflict' element of a narrative arc serves to:
options: Introduce the characters
Create tension that makes the audience care about the outcome
Provide background context
State the moral of the story
quizQuestions.answer: Create tension that makes the audience care about the outcome
quizQuestions.explanation: Conflict is the engine of a story. Without a problem, challenge, or obstacle, there is no reason for the audience to keep listening. Conflict creates stakes and emotional investment.

quizQuestions.question: How should a leader make data compelling through storytelling?
options: Lead with raw numbers and let the audience interpret them
Humanize the data by showing its real-world impact on specific people
Avoid using stories with data to maintain objectivity
Use as many statistics as possible to appear credible
quizQuestions.answer: Humanize the data by showing its real-world impact on specific people
quizQuestions.explanation: A specific, clearly labeled example can show what a statistic may mean in human terms. The example must not be invented as fact or used to claim that one case represents everyone in the dataset.

quizQuestions.question: Which leadership story is most ethically and rhetorically sound?
options: Uses a relevant challenge and lesson while protecting privacy and labeling altered details
Reveals sensitive details because vulnerability is always required
Removes all uncertainty so the leader appears flawless
Changes events to make the speaker's decision look successful
quizQuestions.answer: Uses a relevant challenge and lesson while protecting privacy and labeling altered details
quizQuestions.explanation: A useful story can acknowledge difficulty without forcing disclosure. Ethical storytelling preserves factual boundaries, consent, and privacy while connecting the lesson to the audience's purpose.

quizQuestions.question: Which response best demonstrates reflective paraphrasing during a conversation?
options: 'So you need the current deadline confirmed because the requirements changed—is that accurate?'
'I disagree with your point.'
'I was listening, so there is no need to check my interpretation.'
'Let me change the subject now.'
quizQuestions.answer: 'So you need the current deadline confirmed because the requirements changed—is that accurate?'
quizQuestions.explanation: Reflective paraphrasing restates the message and invites correction. It helps check understanding and signals attention, but accuracy still depends on the speaker confirming or revising the paraphrase.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a common barrier to effective listening?
options: Maintaining open body language
Asking clarifying questions
Formulating your rebuttal while the speaker is still talking
Paraphrasing the speaker's main point
quizQuestions.answer: Formulating your rebuttal while the speaker is still talking
quizQuestions.explanation: Mentally rehearsing a rebuttal divides attention and increases the chance of missing or distorting the speaker's message. 'Pseudo-listening' is a broader label for appearing attentive without genuinely processing the message.

quizQuestions.question: Which response validates a speaker’s emotion without claiming that every interpretation is correct?
options: 'It makes sense that you feel frustrated after receiving conflicting deadline information.'
'You are right, and the coordinator is definitely unfair.'
'There is no reason to feel that way.'
'I understand perfectly, so no clarification is needed.'
quizQuestions.answer: 'It makes sense that you feel frustrated after receiving conflicting deadline information.'
quizQuestions.explanation: Validation acknowledges that an emotion is understandable in the stated context. It does not require agreement with every conclusion, assign blame, or replace clarification of the facts.

quizQuestions.question: A listener notices an unfamiliar facial expression. What should the listener do?
options: Use the cue as one piece of context and ask a neutral clarifying question
Assume the expression proves anger
Ignore all verbal content and rely on body language
Interpret the cue by applying a national stereotype
quizQuestions.answer: Use the cue as one piece of context and ask a neutral clarifying question
quizQuestions.explanation: Nonverbal cues can prompt inquiry but rarely establish a person's emotion or intent by themselves. Clarification reduces mind-reading and respects cultural and individual variation.

quizQuestions.question: Psychological safety in a team is most directly associated with which positive outcome?
options: Lower employee salaries
Increased willingness to take interpersonal risks, share ideas, and admit mistakes
Stricter adherence to rules and procedures
Faster individual task completion
quizQuestions.answer: Increased willingness to take interpersonal risks, share ideas, and admit mistakes
quizQuestions.explanation: Psychological safety concerns whether members believe interpersonal risk-taking is safe. Studies, including Google's internal Project Aristotle analysis, associate it with speaking up and learning; they do not show that it alone guarantees high performance.

quizQuestions.question: Which team communication role is responsible for ensuring all voices are heard and the discussion stays on track?
options: The expert
The devil's advocate
The facilitator
The note-taker
quizQuestions.answer: The facilitator
quizQuestions.explanation: The facilitator manages the process of discussion — distributing speaking time, drawing out quiet members, and keeping the team focused on objectives rather than contributing content.

quizQuestions.question: A communication norm that improves team trust is:
options: Only the leader speaks in meetings
Team members are encouraged to challenge ideas, not people
Disagreements are handled in private, never in team settings
All communication goes through the team leader before reaching teammates
quizQuestions.answer: Team members are encouraged to challenge ideas, not people
quizQuestions.explanation: Separating ideas from people creates a safe environment for debate. This norm encourages intellectual challenge without personal attack, which is essential for innovation.

quizQuestions.question: Which team norm most directly supports psychological safety while preserving accountability?
options: Questions and error reports are acknowledged, examined, and followed by documented next steps
No one may disagree during a meeting
Only the leader may identify mistakes
Every idea must be accepted to protect feelings
quizQuestions.answer: Questions and error reports are acknowledged, examined, and followed by documented next steps
quizQuestions.explanation: The norm makes speaking up visibly useful and pairs openness with action. Psychological safety does not mean avoiding standards, disagreement, or responsibility.

quizQuestions.question: The 'Situation' in the SBI feedback model refers to:
options: A general description of the employee's overall performance
The specific context or event where the observed behavior occurred
The speaker's personal feelings about the behavior
The desired outcome the leader wants to see
quizQuestions.answer: The specific context or event where the observed behavior occurred
quizQuestions.explanation: Anchoring feedback to a specific situation, such as yesterday's team meeting, reduces vagueness and gives both people an event they can examine. It does not by itself guarantee that the feedback is accurate or perceived as fair.

quizQuestions.question: Growth-oriented feedback is distinguished from vague, person-focused criticism primarily because it:
options: Avoids mentioning any negative behaviors
Focuses on behaviors that can be changed and frames improvement as possible
Only praises the person's strengths
Is delivered only in written form
quizQuestions.answer: Focuses on behaviors that can be changed and frames improvement as possible
quizQuestions.explanation: Growth-oriented feedback identifies specific observable behavior and a path for improvement. Vague, person-focused criticism labels the person without giving usable evidence or a change the recipient can act on.

quizQuestions.question: After receiving feedback, what is the most evidence-based first evaluation?
options: Check whether the feedback identifies a specific event, observable behavior, and credible impact
Accept every claim immediately to avoid appearing defensive
Reject the message if its tone feels uncomfortable
Infer the giver's intent before checking the facts
quizQuestions.answer: Check whether the feedback identifies a specific event, observable behavior, and credible impact
quizQuestions.explanation: Specificity and evidence help the recipient separate useful information from general labels. Tone and source matter, but neither automatic acceptance nor automatic rejection is required.

quizQuestions.question: The Thomas-Kilmann conflict model assesses conflict styles on two dimensions. What are they?
options: Speed and accuracy
Assertiveness and cooperativeness
Verbal and nonverbal communication
Task focus and relationship focus
quizQuestions.answer: Assertiveness and cooperativeness
quizQuestions.explanation: The TKI model plots conflict styles on two axes: assertiveness (concern for own needs) and cooperativeness (concern for others' needs). The five styles result from different combinations of these.

quizQuestions.question: What makes interest-based negotiation different from positional bargaining?
options: Focuses on what is demanded rather than why
Seeks the underlying needs behind stated positions
Always results in compromise
Requires a neutral third-party mediator
quizQuestions.answer: Seeks the underlying needs behind stated positions
quizQuestions.explanation: Positional bargaining ('I want X') is rigid and zero-sum. Interest-based approaches ('Why do you want X?') reveal underlying needs that often have creative, mutually beneficial solutions.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following phrases is an example of de-escalation language in a difficult conversation?
options: 'You always do this and it needs to stop.'
'I want to understand your perspective — can you help me see it from your side?'
'This is your fault and I have the evidence to prove it.'
'If you don't change, there will be consequences.'
quizQuestions.answer: 'I want to understand your perspective — can you help me see it from your side?'
quizQuestions.explanation: De-escalation language is curious, non-blaming, and invites collaboration. It lowers defensive reactions and moves both parties from opposition toward dialogue.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement applies the Thomas-Kilmann model most responsibly?
options: Use assertiveness and cooperativeness to describe options, then consider safety, stakes, time, and power
Collaborating is always the only ethical style
Avoiding always shows weak leadership
A style label predicts the outcome without other evidence
quizQuestions.answer: Use assertiveness and cooperativeness to describe options, then consider safety, stakes, time, and power
quizQuestions.explanation: The model is a descriptive map of five modes along two dimensions. Appropriate use requires context; it does not rank one style as universally best or predict success by itself.
